I. What will you remember Asrani for? Sholay? Abhimaan? Since the death of the veteran actor
was announced, a lot of obituaries and fan-posts on social media have mentioned his iconic
dialogue from Sholay “Hum angrezon ke zamane ke jailer hain” (I am a jailor of the British
era). Asrani acted in more than 300 films in Hindi and Gujarati. Some small, some big.Despite
such a mammoth filmography, if we choose to remember an actor for a specific role/dialogue
from one film, it says something about our viewing of an actor’s body of work. It means that
we have normalised stereotyping him to such an extent that it doesn’t even seem discordant
anymore. Imagine the disappointment of the actor who is remembered for one role despite a
vast filmography, while marginalising everything else he has done on screen!

On TV shows and public events, Asrani was constantly asked to mouth the Sholay dialogue,
sometimes to his irritation, which he didn’t hide. This dialogue is also entrenched in public
memory because repetition doesn’t allow forgetting. Actors play along to not appear rude and
to entertain their fans and stay in the public memory. This also seems the perfect illustration of
the stereotyping of an actor by the industry, which, in turn, gets entrenched in public
imagination, so much so that you refuse to think of the actor beyond that particular point of
reference. Asrani is one of the many who unwillingly submitted to this stereotype of the funny,
comic actor. He could carry those roles with elan, but what other choice did Asrani have? To
survive in the industry, you perform what is given to you. Audiences are the losers when an
actor is boxed into a slot and denied the opportunity to essay a wide array of roles. Asrani
became a perennial comic.
The Asrani story also makes us think about the fate of an actor in Hindi cinema. That so little
of your filmography is under your control, especially when you don’t look a certain way. The
Bollywood hero has to subscribe to a pre-determined template. When you don’t conform to the
template, you become a character actor — another coinage that makes no sense. Every actor,
including the lead of the film, is playing a character. So why divide and relegate? Here again,
Asrani did not have a choice.

questions.stimulus:
II. Everyone warned me about my new neighbourhood before I moved in. “Not safe.” “Too
immigrant.” “A no-go area.” The labels came thick and casual, like weather talk. I had just
landed in Germany with two squeaky suitcases and a folder full of proofs of existence —
contracts, passport photos, bank statements — ready to start a fellowship in Berlin. I signed the
lease anyway.
My flat is in Neukölln, a district in south Berlin where many Arab and Turkish families have
built their lives over decades. Think of it as the Malviya Nagar of Delhi or Park Circus of
Kolkata — dense, diverse, argumentative, generous. If you’ve never been to Germany, picture
kebab shops and bakeries lining long, straight roads; a wide canal cutting through like a green
ribbon; the metro train — breathing people up and down stairways; and languages braided in
the air —German, Arabic, Turkish, English, and the shy Bengali I carry inside me.
On my first evening, the street met me like a crowded family photo. A football rolled into a
florist’s bucket; roses rocked; the boy apologised; the shopkeeper laughed. A bakery slid open
its shutter; the air filled with sesame and cardamom. The phrase “no-go” didn’t fit anywhere in
my head. In those early days, I learned more German from shopkeepers than from any app. At
the corner store, a cheerful “Kartenzahlung?”— card payment? — taught me how to pay
without holding up the line. At the grocer’s, the aunty weighed parsley and slipped mint into
my bag “for tea, Geschenk”— a gift. At the barber, “Habibi, next week—fresh cut!”.
Berlin’s bureaucracy is famous, and it arrived in my mailbox with insurance letters,
registrations, deadlines. When one envelope stumped me, I carried it to the corner shop like a
broken toy. The owner read it carefully, made two phone calls, and dictated my reply. When I
offered a chocolate bar in thanks, he waved it away. “Neighbour,” he said. That one word did
what no glossy “Welcome to Berlin” brochure could. The longer I live here, the more I think
the only true “no-go” zone is the temptation to speak about a neighbourhood without letting it
speak back. I learned neighbourliness by doing it, until it settled in my muscles: holding
parcels, translating letters, swapping recipes, noticing when a routine goes quiet. Home, and
even the address I claim, isn’t a certificate; it’s the people who answer when I knock.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns/germany-immigrants-berlin-
who-is-my-neighbour-neighbourhood-10320831/

IV. Little Mrs. Sommers one day found herself the unexpected possessor of fifteen dollars. It
seemed to her a very large amount of money, and the way in which it stuffed and bulged her
worn old porte-monnaie gave her a feeling of importance such as she had not enjoyed for years.
The question of investment was one that occupied her greatly. For a day or two she walked
about apparently in a dreamy state, but really absorbed in speculation and calculation. She did
not wish to act hastily, to do anything she might afterward regret. But it was during the still
hours of the night when she lay awake revolving plans in her mind that she seemed to see her
way clearly toward a proper and judicious use of the money.
A dollar or two should be added to the price usually paid for Janie's shoes, which would insure
their lasting an appreciable time longer than they usually did. She would buy so and so many
yards of percale for new shirt waists for the boys and Janie and Mag. She had intended to make
the old ones do by skilful patching. Mag should have another gown. She had seen some
beautiful patterns, veritable bargains in the shop windows. And still there would be left enough
for new stockings--two pairs apiece--and what darning that would save for a while! She would
get caps for the boys and sailor-hats for the girls. The vision of her little brood looking fresh
and dainty and new for once in their lives excited her and made her restless and wakeful with
anticipation.

before she had ever thought of being Mrs. Sommers. She herself indulged in no such morbid
retrospection. She had no time--no second of time to devote to the past. The needs of the present
absorbed her every faculty. A vision of the future like some dim, gaunt monster sometimes
appalled her, but luckily tomorrow never comes.

criteria must be met for a financial market boom to be classified as a bubble. One, investors

consensus that the object of investor pursuit is the next big thing. Three, returns on investment
become unanchored from earnings. The market frenzy over AI satisfies all three criteria.

Legal Reasoning


XI. The genesis of India's Constitution lies in the historic deliberations of its Constituent
Assembly. A critical legal and historical fact is that this Assembly was not a spontaneous
creation but was established under a specific constitutional framework. Contrary to common
misconception, it was not formed by the Indian Independence Act of 1947, though that act later
granted it sovereign power. The Assembly's foundational basis was also not the prevailing
Government of India Act of 1935, which it was meant to replace, nor was it the Objectives
Resolution, which was one of its own early products. Rather, the Constituent Assembly was
concretely set up under the provisions of the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946. This Plan,
formulated by three British ministers, proposed the composition and method of election for the
Assembly, envisioning it as the body to draft a constitution for a united India. Thus, its very
existence and initial structure were derived from this 1946 plan.


Following this framework, the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was convened on
December 9, 1946. The session was marked by the notable absence of members from the
Muslim League, who boycotted the proceedings. Despite this significant political challenge
and the shadow of impending partition, the Assembly's work began. The most immediate and
crucial outcome of this inaugural session was not the adoption of the National Flag or the
Objectives Resolution, both of which occurred in later sessions, nor was it the appointment of
the Drafting Committee, which came much later in August 1947. The paramount achievement
was the election of Dr. Rajendra Prasad as the Permanent President of the Assembly on
December 11, 1946. This election provided the Assembly with stable and respected leadership,
ensuring its procedural continuity and legitimacy at a very fragile moment. By successfully
constituting itself with a permanent presiding officer, the Assembly demonstrated its
operational viability and set the essential administrative foundation for the monumental task
ahead, navigating the complex journey from a British blueprint to an independent Republic.

questions.stimulus:
XII. A breach of contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, triggers a suite of remedial
options for the aggrieved party, primarily outlined in Sections 73 to 75. These provisions
establish a comprehensive framework designed not to punish the defaulting party, but to
compensate the injured party for the loss suffered and, where possible, to uphold the sanctity
of the original agreement.


The principal remedy is an award of damages under Section 73. The foundational principle is
to place the plaintiff in the same financial position they would have occupied had the contract
been performed. This covers ordinary damages, which arise naturally in the usual course of
events from the breach. For special damages—losses arising from the plaintiff’s particular
circumstances—the defendant must have had knowledge, actual or imputed, of those
circumstances at the time of contract formation, ensuring the loss was within the parties’
contemplation. Section 74 addresses liquidated damages, a genuine pre-estimate of loss
stipulated in the contract itself. The critical distinction lies in the court’s treatment of a penalty,
which is a stipulation in terrorem to secure performance. While Section 74 permits recovery of
the stipulated sum whether termed penalty or damages, the amount awarded is limited to the
court’s assessment of the actual loss or injury proved, never exceeding the stipulated figure,
thereby neutralizing penal consequences.


Beyond monetary compensation, equitable remedies seek to enforce performance directly.
Specific Performance, governed by the Specific Relief Act, 1963, is a discretionary decree
ordering the defendant to execute their contractual promise, typically granted where damages
are inadequate, as in contracts concerning unique property. Similarly, an Injunction, a
restraining order, prevents a party from committing a breach negative in nature, such as
violating a non-compete covenant.


Finally, the doctrine of Quantum Meruit operates on principles of quasi-contract to prevent
unjust enrichment. Where a contract is discharged by breach or becomes void, and a party has
executed a part, they can claim reasonable remuneration for the work done or benefits
conferred. This ensures fairness, allowing recovery for value delivered even in the absence of
a fully executed agreement. Together, these remedies under Sections 73-75 provide a balanced
and just system for addressing contractual breaches, blending compensatory, deterrent, and
restorative principles.

XIII. The Indian Constitution establishes a bicameral Union Parliament, comprising the
directly elected Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States),
representing the states. State legislatures are predominantly unicameral, with a few retaining a
Legislative Council as their upper house. These bodies wield the core legislative power of the
Union and States respectively, as demarcated by the Seventh Schedule’s Union, State, and
Concurrent Lists. Beyond lawmaking, they exercise critical financial control through the
sanction of expenditures and taxation, and hold the executive accountable via mechanisms like
questions, debates, and no-confidence motions. To ensure fearless deliberation, legislators
enjoy constitutional privileges under Articles 105 and 194, including freedom of speech within
the house and immunity from prosecution for official proceedings, powers essential for
parliamentary autonomy.


The legislative procedure involves introduction, consideration, and passage of bills in each
house, with the President’s or Governor’s assent required for enactment. A critical exception is
the Money Bill, stringently defined under Article 110. Certified exclusively by the Lok Sabha
Speaker, such bills deal solely with specified financial matters like taxation or Consolidated
Fund expenditure. Their introduction is restricted to the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can
only recommend amendments; the lower house holds the final authority, reinforcing the
primacy of the directly elected house in financial legislation. To curb political instability, the
Tenth Schedule (Anti-defection Law) disqualifies members on grounds of voluntarily giving
up party membership or defying a whip on a vote, aiming to preserve the electoral mandate’s
sanctity, though its application has raised complex questions regarding legislative
independence.


The dynamic between parliamentary sovereignty and constitutional supremacy is central to
India’s framework. Unlike the UK, India’s Parliament is not supreme. It operates within limits
set by a written, rigid Constitution, which is the supreme lex. This is vividly demonstrated by
Article 13, which voids laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights, and the Basic Structure
Doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), which holds that Parliament’s amending power under


Article 368 cannot alter the Constitution’s foundational identity. Thus, while Parliament
possesses expansive legislative and constituent powers, its authority is subordinated to and
constrained by the Constitution, with the judiciary acting as the ultimate interpreter and
guardian of this supreme document, ensuring a delicate balance of power among the sovereign
organs of the state.

The Lok Sabha introduces a bill that imposes a fine for environmental violations, with
    the collected money going to a dedicated national green fund. The Speaker certifies it
    as a Money Bill. The Rajya Sabha proposes an amendment to change the adjudicating
    authority for the fine. Can the Lok Sabha disregard this amendment and present the

      the amendment due to matters of pressing national environmental importance.

A State Legislative Assembly passes an ordinary law that restricts public gatherings in
    certain areas. The State High Court strikes down the law, declaring it violates the
    fundamental right to peaceful assembly. The State Legislature, in response, re-passes
    the exact same law with a simple majority, stating the judiciary cannot bind the
    sovereign legislature. Is this re-enactment constitutionally valid?

options.text:
No, because once a law is declared unconstitutional for violating fundamental
      rights, it is nullified, and the same law cannot be re-enacted without rectifying the
      violation.

options.text:
Yes, but only if the law is now passed by a special majority to give it greater
      legitimacy and insulate it from further judicial review processes.

options.text:
No, because all State laws require the prior approval of the Union Parliament
      when they have been previously invalidated by a High Court's ruling on
      constitutionality.

options.text:
Yes, the legislature is sovereign within its domain and can re-enact a law to assert
      its legislative authority and policy preference over judicial opinion.

    the fall of the existing government. The MP claims their defection was justified due to

questions.stimulus:
XIV. In a landmark judgment reshaping India's reservation jurisprudence, the Supreme Court
has unequivocally permitted states to enact laws creating sub-classifications within the lists of
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes for the purpose of distributing reservation benefits.
This ruling fundamentally recalibrates the balance of power between the legislature and the
judiciary on a deeply sensitive social justice issue. At the heart of this legal shift is the Court's
decisive overturning of its own 2004 precedent in E.V. Chinnaiah vs. State of Andhra Pradesh.


The Chinnaiah judgment, delivered by a five-judge Constitution Bench, had imposed a
significant restriction on state authority. It held that the Scheduled Castes, as notified under
Articles 341 and 342 of the Constitution, constituted a single, homogeneous class for the
purpose of Article 16(4). The Court reasoned that any sub-division by a state legislature would
violate the constitutional scheme and the right to equality under Article 14. This precedent had
effectively frozen state-level attempts to ensure that the most backward among the SCs/STs
received a fair share of reservation benefits, as it mandated that all communities within the list
must be treated identically.


The recent verdict, delivered by a seven-judge bench, dismantles this legal barrier. It
authoritatively holds that the Chinnaiah judgment was incorrectly decided. The Court has now
ruled that there is no constitutional prohibition against sub-classification. It affirmed that
inequalities within the SC/ST communities themselves are a stark social reality. When some
groups within these lists have historically cornered a disproportionate share of the reservation
benefits, leaving others in continued backwardness, the state has both a right and a positive
obligation to rectify this internal imbalance. This power, the Court clarified, flows from the
legislature's competence to determine the adequacy of representation under Article 16(4) and
to promote substantive equality. By overturning Chinnaiah, the Supreme Court has restored to
state governments a vital tool for fine-tuning reservation policies to achieve equitable
distribution, moving beyond a one-size-fits-all approach to a more nuanced, needs-based model
for social justice.

has unequivocally permitted states to enact laws creating sub-classifications within the lists of

XV. The legal landscape for transgender rights in India has been fundamentally shaped by the
Supreme Court's landmark 2014 ruling in National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v.
Union of India. This judgment expansively interpreted Article 21 of the Constitution, holding
that the right to life and personal liberty inherently includes the right to one's gender identity,
autonomy, and dignity. By recognizing transgender persons as a third gender, the Court
mandated their legal recognition and directed the Centre and State Governments to treat them
as socially and educationally backward classes (OBCs). This pivotal direction made them
eligible for reservation in education and public employment under the existing OBC quota,
rather than creating a separate, fixed-percentage category. This classification was aimed at
providing substantive equality and affirmative action to a historically marginalized community.


However, the subsequent Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, introduced
provisions that many activists and experts argue regress from the NALSA principles. A widely
criticized feature is the process for obtaining a certificate of identity. Contrary to the self-
determination model affirmed by the Supreme Court, the Act requires an application to the
District Magistrate, who issues a certificate based on a recommendation from a district
screening committee. This medicalized and bureaucratic process is seen as infringing upon the
dignity and autonomy guaranteed by NALSA.

Kumar v. Inspector General of Registration (2022), the Madras High Court addressed the
crucial right to marry. It held that a marriage between a cisgender man and a transgender
woman who had not undergone gender-confirmation surgery constitutes a valid heterosexual
marriage under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. This reasoning, building on a similar 2019 ruling
from the same court, validated such unions without requiring explicit legislative amendment,
grounding the right in the constitutional values of equality, dignity, and privacy established in
the NALSA verdict. Collectively, this jurisprudence underscores an ongoing tension between
progressive constitutional interpretation and legislative measures that are perceived as falling
short of guaranteeing full self-determination.

questions.stimulus:
XVI. The statutory framework governing Christian succession in India, primarily enshrined in
the Indian Succession Act, 1925, extends beyond the standard rules of intestate and
testamentary distribution to address specific, often complex, situational doctrines. These
provisions resolve ambiguities and address the status of individuals who occupy a peripheral
position under the default inheritance scheme.


A critical aspect is the succession to a minor’s property. As a minor lacks the legal capacity to
manage assets, the estate of a deceased Christian minor does not vest directly in their natural
guardian. Instead, its administration is governed by the secular Guardians and Wards Act, 1890.
The court, prioritizing the welfare of the minor, will appoint a guardian to manage the inherited
property prudently until the minor attains the age of majority, ensuring the estate is preserved
for their ultimate benefit.


The law adopts a distinct approach towards illegitimate children. Under the Act’s intestacy
rules, an illegitimate child possesses no legal right to inherit from the father’s estate. This
restrictive stance is, however, partially mitigated by the child’s right to succeed to the mother’s
property on her intestacy. Importantly, the principle of testamentary freedom allows a father to
expressly bequeath property to an illegitimate child through a valid will, thereby circumventing
the statutory exclusion.


The doctrine of commorientes addresses the rare but legally significant scenario of
simultaneous death. When two individuals, such as a husband and wife, perish in a common
disaster where the sequence of death cannot be ascertained, Section 21 of the Act establishes a
legal presumption for succession purposes: the younger is deemed to have survived the elder.
This presumption, while crucial for determining the line of inheritance, is rebuttable by direct
evidence proving the actual order of death.


A fundamental principle of property law, escheat, applies when a Christian dies intestate
without leaving any heir identifiable under the succession hierarchy of the Act. In such an
event, where no natural or legal person is entitled to claim the estate, the property does not
remain in abeyance but instead devolves upon the state, thereby preventing title from becoming
dormant.


Finally, the applicability of these rules is profoundly influenced by the concept of domicile.
Succession to movable property for an Indian Christian is governed by the law of their domicile
at the time of death. Consequently, a Christian of Indian origin domiciled abroad may have the
succession to their movable assets determined by foreign law, while their immovable property
in India remains subject to the Indian Succession Act, creating a potential conflict of laws
scenario that requires careful legal navigation within this codified personal law system.

The results are not good. As democracy fades in many places, corruption is getting worse. The
United Kingdom is sliding down the rankings.

happened under Boris Johnson. And all of this was before the latest problems involving Peter
Mandelson. Unless things change quickly, next year’s report will likely be even worse.

and again to “clean up politics.” But his government got off to a bad start. Some of his team
accepted free clothes and tickets to events. They declared these gifts properly, but it still looked
bad. One study found that top Labour officials accepted over £220,000 worth of free tickets
during the last few years. These included tickets to Glastonbury, Wimbledon, and the British
Grand Prix.


These gifts seem small compared to bigger scandals. During the pandemic, the government
handed out billions in contracts. Watchdogs found serious problems in about a third of that
spending. They said it looked like more than just bad luck or mistakes.

government for a bank that later went bust. And George Osborne, another former minister, has
taken many well-paid jobs since leaving office. None of this is illegal. But it makes people
wonder if politicians are working for the public or for themselves.

the truth. Fewer believe they put the country first. The small gifts to ministers only made things
worse. At a time when politics already feels broken, every little bit of bad news adds up.

questions.stimulus:
XXI. Your fingers might tell a surprising story about the human brain. New research suggests
that the length of your fingers, specifically how they compare to each other, could be linked to
how our brains evolved.


Scientists have long known that human brains have grown larger over time. A new study points
to a possible reason: a hormone called estrogen that babies are exposed to before they are born.


The study focuses on something called the "digit ratio." This is simply a comparison of your
index finger (the one you use to point) and your ring finger. Scientists call this the 2D:4D ratio.


Here is what they have learned. When a baby is growing in the womb, it is exposed to hormones
like estrogen and testosterone. If the baby gets more estrogen relative to testosterone during
the first three months, the index finger tends to be longer than the ring finger. This is called a
high 2D:4D ratio. If there is more testosterone, the ring finger is usually longer, which is a low
ratio.


For this new study, researchers wanted to see if this finger ratio was connected to brain size.
Since the size of a newborn's head is a good way to estimate brain size, they measured the
heads and fingers of 225 babies. The group had 100 boys and 125 girls.


The results showed a clear pattern, but only in the boys. Baby boys with a higher 2D:4D ratio
(meaning more estrogen before birth) also had larger heads. This link was not found in girls.


So, what does this mean for human evolution? Professor John Manning from Swansea
University explains that the drive to have a bigger brain may have come with a trade-off. High
estrogen levels in males (shown by their finger ratio) are also linked to some health issues, like
heart problems, low sperm counts, and a higher risk of schizophrenia.


But a larger brain may have been so important for survival that it made up for these problems.
In other words, the evolution of the human brain may have been helped by the very same
hormone that causes some health risks in men.


This study adds to the idea that the hormone estrogen, received before birth, played a key role
in shaping the human brain, even if it came with some biological costs.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Scientists find a clue to human brain evolution in
finger length”, ScienceDaily.]
